headline: Issue and request the TLS Feature extension, hold a chain to the features its issuer advertises, and read a parsed destination through accessors taken at load.
summary: The RFC 7633 TLS Feature extension, the must-staple declaration, has been readable since v0.8.11 and is now writable: a certificate or a certification request takes `extensions.tlsFeature` as a list of TLS ExtensionType values, by number or by registry name. What the values mean is the IANA registry's business rather than the syntax's, so the encoder emits what it is given and a new lint profile reports a value outside the registry's width, a repeat, the transparency_info feature a certification authority is asked not to issue, and the feature TLS 1.3 no longer defines. Path validation now enforces the one requirement in RFC 7633 that certificate bytes can decide: a certificate issued under a signing certificate that advertises features must offer the same set or a superset.

Added: `extensions.tlsFeature` on `pki.x509.sign`, `pki.csr.sign` and `pki.x509.extension` writes the RFC 7633 TLS Feature extension. The value is a list of TLS ExtensionType values, each a number, a bigint, or one of the registry names this build knows, `status_request` and `status_request_v2`. It is emitted non-critical unless `tlsFeatureCritical` is set: section 4 says the extension SHOULD NOT be marked critical and then names the case where the critical form is the intent, so the knob exists rather than the critical form being refused. A request carries it in the certification-request extension attribute, which is where OpenSSL's `req -addext "tlsfeature=status_request"` puts it, and the bytes the two produce are identical. An empty list is refused, because the extension it would emit advertises nothing; one that arrives on the wire still decodes, as it did before.

`pki.lint.certificate(der, { profile: "rfc7633" })` reads the extension's values. RFC 7633 states no range, no ordering and no prohibition on repeats, so none of those is refused by the encoder and all are reported here: a feature outside the 16-bit width of the IANA registry that section 4.1 points at, and a repeated feature, which names the same set it would without the repeat. Two rows come from elsewhere. RFC 9162 section 7.2 asks a certification authority not to issue a certificate naming the transparency_info feature, because a TLS server need not support it to take part in certificate transparency. And a certificate naming status_request_v2 asks of a TLS 1.3 server something that version does not define: RFC 9846 obsoletes RFC 6961, which defined that extension, and leaves it out of the ExtensionType enum in its section 4.3. The IANA registry still lists it as recommended and marks it neither obsolete nor deprecated, so that row is a notice and says only what those documents say. A critical TLS Feature extension is reported by the default rule set and needs no profile.

`pki.path.validate` enforces RFC 7633 section 4.2.2 at every issuer-to-subject boundary of a path. A certificate signed by a signing certificate that asserts keyCertSign and carries the extension must carry one offering the same set or a superset, or the path fails with `path/tls-feature-not-offered`; a subject carrying no extension at all under such an issuer is the same failure, because the clause requires it to carry one. The comparison is of sets, so neither order nor a repeat on either side changes it. An issuer that carries no extension constrains nothing. A trust anchor's own extensions are not read, so the rule applies from the first certificate in the path downward, and a boundary that was not checked reports no result rather than a passing one.
Fixed: A parsed request destination is read through accessors the package captured at load, in `pki.acme`, `pki.est`, `pki.scep`, `pki.cmp`, the revocation fetcher, the certificate-path builder's authority-information-access fetch and the HTTP transport's Digest authentication. Capturing the `URL` constructor, which v0.8.50 did, does not capture the prototype the value it returns reads its parts off: redefining `href` there answered every read of a destination, so a caller's code running mid-request could still move it. Each part is now read once into a local and every decision made from that local, which also closes the case of a part that answers two reads differently: the scheme that decides whether a request is allowed is the scheme the port defaults from, the host the address filter is applied to is the host the request is sent to, and the request target a Digest credential is computed over is the target it is sent to.

The citation on the TLS Feature renderer named RFC 7633 section 6 for the ExtensionType values. Section 6 is IANA Considerations and registers the extension's own object identifier; section 4.1 is the clause that points at the IANA registry for the values.
